title: Week 19 · Lesson 43: Neurologic Pharmacology — Headache, Migraine, Seizure & Neuropathic Pain
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 19 — Lesson 43: Neurologic Pharmacology — Headache, Migraine, Seizure & Neuropathic Pain

FNP-level goal: Treat common neurologic symptoms with a diagnosis-first approach that distinguishes a stable primary disorder from a neurologic emergency, selects medication around patient-specific risk, and creates a follow-up plan for efficacy, safety, and referral.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate primary headache syndromes from red-flag secondary headache before medication selection.
  • Compare acute and preventive migraine medication strategies without using medication as a substitute for diagnosis.
  • Recognize medication-overuse headache and build a safe reassessment plan.
  • Apply antiseizure-medication safety principles, including adherence, interactions, and reproductive counseling.
  • Explain why neuropathic pain often needs a mechanism-based treatment plan rather than escalating conventional analgesics.

Part 1 — The First Headache Question Is Not “Which Drug?”

Before selecting a headache medication, decide whether this is a familiar, stable primary headache pattern or a possible secondary headache. A new sudden severe headache, focal neurologic deficit, altered mental status, fever with meningeal symptoms, papilledema/vision change, pregnancy or postpartum risk context, cancer/immunocompromise, major head trauma, exertional onset, or a clear pattern change requires urgent diagnostic thinking.

“This feels like my migraine” can be reassuring only when the history is truly consistent and the examination/context do not raise concern. Medication must never delay emergency evaluation for suspected stroke, hemorrhage, meningitis, hypertensive emergency, acute angle-closure glaucoma, venous thrombosis, or another dangerous cause.

Part 2 — Build a Headache Phenotype

Migraine commonly produces recurrent attacks with moderate-to-severe, often pulsating pain plus nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, worsened activity, and sometimes aura. Tension-type headache is often bilateral and pressing/tightening without the same migrainous symptom burden. Cluster headache is a distinct syndrome characterized by severe unilateral attacks with autonomic features and needs a specific diagnostic and treatment pathway.

Do not use a medication response as the sole diagnostic test. Record frequency, duration, disability, aura, acute-medication use, triggers, sleep, menstrual/reproductive context, blood pressure, neurologic symptoms, and prior imaging or specialist history when relevant.

Part 3 — Acute Migraine Therapy: Match the Drug to the Attack and Patient

Acute treatment may include nonopioid analgesics, antiemetics, triptans, CGRP-pathway agents, ditans, or other options depending on diagnosis, attack severity, prior response, contraindications, interactions, and current labeling. The correct choice is not the “strongest” drug; it is the safest evidence-based option for that patient and attack.

Ask about vascular disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, pregnancy, liver/kidney disease, serotonergic medications, sedatives, work/driving needs, and all OTC combination products. A patient with new chest symptoms or an unclear headache diagnosis needs assessment—not an automatic repeat dose.

Part 4 — Triptans: Understand the Vascular and Interaction Context

Triptans are migraine-specific acute therapies for selected patients. Their appropriateness depends on the clinical diagnosis and cardiovascular/cerebrovascular risk context, as well as the specific product labeling. They are not a treatment for a possible stroke, atypical acute neurologic event, or unexplained new severe headache.

Perform medication reconciliation for serotonergic agents and educate patients to seek assessment for concerning systemic symptoms. Use the current label and patient-specific risk assessment rather than memorizing one universal rule for every person with migraine.

Part 5 — Medication-Overuse Headache: More Medication Can Mean More Headache

Frequent acute-medication use can transform episodic attacks into near-daily or increasingly frequent headache. This is medication-overuse headache. A headache diary is a clinical tool: it reveals headache days, acute-treatment days, disability, triggers, and whether the treatment plan is creating a rebound cycle.

Do not simply add another rescue drug. Reconfirm the diagnosis, identify every analgesic and combination product, discuss a supervised reduction strategy when needed, and consider whether preventive treatment, specialist support, or a different acute option is appropriate. Sudden discontinuation may not be appropriate for every medication class or patient.

Part 6 — Prevention Is About Disability and Burden

Preventive migraine therapy may be considered when attacks are frequent, disabling, prolonged, poorly responsive to acute treatment, or when acute therapy is contraindicated or overused. Options include selected antihypertensives, antiseizure medications, antidepressant-class agents, CGRP-targeting therapies, and other modality-specific treatments.

Choose prevention around comorbidity and risk. For example, a medication may affect blood pressure, heart rate, cognition, mood, weight, pregnancy planning, kidney-stone risk, or drug interactions. Set a measurable goal—fewer headache days, less disability, less rescue-medication use—and reassess rather than continuing a medication indefinitely without outcome data.

Part 7 — Seizure Pharmacology Begins With Seizure Safety

An episode of loss of awareness, convulsive movement, collapse, or unusual behavior is not automatically epilepsy. Syncope, arrhythmia, hypoglycemia, intoxication/withdrawal, stroke, infection, psychogenic events, and medication effects can mimic or provoke seizures. Obtain a detailed witness history, timeline, injuries, recovery phase, medical context, and medication/substance history.

First seizure, prolonged seizure activity, repeated seizures without recovery, pregnancy, trauma, focal deficits, persistent altered mental status, fever/meningeal symptoms, or serious metabolic concern requires urgent evaluation. Do not start or change chronic antiseizure treatment from an incomplete event description alone.

Part 8 — Antiseizure Medication: Adherence Is a Safety Intervention

For a diagnosed seizure disorder, missed doses, vomiting, pharmacy barriers, sleep deprivation, alcohol/substance exposure, and drug interactions can all increase breakthrough-seizure risk. Ask nonjudgmentally about adherence and access before labeling a medication ineffective.

Antiseizure medications differ substantially in adverse effects, interaction profiles, required monitoring, and reproductive considerations. Abrupt discontinuation can precipitate seizures in some circumstances. Any change should follow the treating clinician’s plan, current labeling, and appropriate neurology collaboration.

Part 9 — Reproductive Planning Is Not an Optional Footnote

For patients with epilepsy who could become pregnant, ask early about pregnancy intentions and contraception. The safest plan balances seizure control against medication-specific fetal and maternal risks. Preconception counseling, folic-acid guidance, medication review, and neurology/obstetric collaboration should occur before pregnancy whenever possible.

Do not tell a patient to stop an antiseizure medication because of a positive pregnancy test without urgent coordination. Uncontrolled seizures can also create serious risk. The clinical task is timely expert-supported risk balancing.

Part 10 — Neuropathic Pain: Treat the Mechanism

Neuropathic pain may be burning, electric, shooting, tingling, or associated with allodynia and sensory loss. Causes include diabetes, postherpetic neuralgia, radiculopathy, chemotherapy exposure, alcohol use, vitamin deficiency, entrapment neuropathy, and central nervous-system disease. Identify the likely cause while treating symptoms.

Conventional analgesics may have limited benefit for neuropathic mechanisms. Selected antidepressant-class agents, gabapentinoids, topical therapies, and other options can be considered based on diagnosis, renal function, sedation/fall risk, mood, interactions, misuse risk, and functional goals. Do not escalate sedating medications without reassessing gait, cognition, respiratory risk, and concurrent opioids or alcohol.

Part 11 — Gabapentinoids: Useful for Some Patients, Not Risk-Free

Gabapentinoids can cause dizziness, sedation, cognitive effects, and fall risk; dosing and safety are influenced by kidney function and co-administered CNS depressants. A prescription does not replace treatment of the underlying neuropathy, foot care in diabetes, fall prevention, or evaluation of weakness, bowel/bladder change, rapidly progressive symptoms, or new asymmetry.

For patients receiving opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol, or other sedatives, assess combined CNS/respiratory risk carefully. Functional benefit—not only a numerical pain score—should guide continued therapy.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Headache With Red Flags

A 54-year-old with no prior migraine history develops the worst headache of life during exertion, followed by vomiting and neck pain.

FNP reasoning: sudden maximal onset and a new severe pattern are red flags. This requires emergency evaluation for secondary causes; it is not a routine outpatient migraine prescription.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: The Rebound Cycle

A patient with a past migraine diagnosis now has headache 18 days each month and uses a combination OTC analgesic or triptan on many days.

FNP reasoning: assess medication-overuse headache, attack frequency, diagnoses, all products, blood pressure, sleep, mood, and disability. A diary and an individualized plan to reduce overuse and consider prevention are safer than repeatedly authorizing rescue therapy.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: “Breakthrough Seizures”

A patient with established epilepsy reports two seizures after a viral illness with vomiting. They have missed several antiseizure doses and cannot keep fluids down.

FNP reasoning: assess immediate safety, prolonged/recurrent seizure activity, injury, hydration, metabolic issues, and medication access. Illness and missed medication can be clinically important triggers. Coordinate urgent evaluation and the established seizure-care team rather than improvising a chronic regimen.

Part 15 — Clinical Case: Burning Feet in Diabetes

A patient with diabetes reports burning feet, sleep disruption, reduced sensation, and two recent near-falls. They request “a stronger pain pill.”

FNP reasoning: confirm the phenotype, examine feet and neurologic function, assess glucose control, footwear/injury risk, kidney function, alcohol/substances, concurrent sedatives, and function. Build a mechanism-based plan with safety and fall prevention rather than reflexive opioid escalation.

FNP Neurologic Pharmacology Framework

  1. Decide whether the presentation has a red flag requiring emergency or urgent neurologic evaluation.
  2. Define the syndrome and exclude important mimics before selecting a class of medication.
  3. Reconcile every prescription, OTC product, supplement, and substance exposure.
  4. Choose acute treatment by diagnosis, severity, contraindications, interactions, and patient function.
  5. Use diaries and measurable outcomes to identify overuse, disability, and need for prevention.
  6. For seizures and neuropathic pain, protect safety, adherence, reproductive health, cognition, gait, and functional outcomes.

High-Yield Summary

New or thunderclap headache: evaluate for secondary causes before treating as migraine.
Migraine: acute and preventive therapy must match diagnosis, burden, comorbidity, and current product labeling.
Medication-overuse headache: frequent rescue medication can worsen headache frequency; use a diary and reassess the plan.
Seizure medications: adherence, interactions, abrupt discontinuation, and reproductive planning are major safety issues.
Neuropathic pain: treat the mechanism and underlying cause; monitor sedation, kidney function, falls, and functional benefit.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Neurologic diagnosis, imaging decisions, medication selection, dosing, pregnancy counseling, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, FDA-approved prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
